claim: Prions replicate via the autocatalytic conversion of cellular prion protein (PrPC) into fibrillar assemblies of misfolded PrP.
source: Prions replicate via the autocatalytic conversion of cellular prion protein (PrPC) into fibrillar assemblies of misfolded PrP.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about prion replication mechanisms.

claim: Non-physiological reaction conditions of fibril formation in vitro have precluded the identification and mechanistic analysis of cellular proteins which may alter PrP self-assembly and prion replication.
source: While this process has been extensively studied in vivo and in vitro, non-physiological reaction conditions of fibril formation in vitro have precluded the identification and mechanistic analysis of cellular proteins, which may alter PrP self-assembly and prion replication.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the limitations of existing experimental methods.

claim: Variants that increase syntaxin-6 expression in the brain are risk factors for sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.
source: Genetic screening suggests that variants that increase syntaxin-6 expression in the brain (gene: STX6) are risk factors for sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to genetic screening studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 is a potent inhibitor of PrP fibril formation.
source: Analysis of the protein in NAA revealed, counterintuitively, that syntaxin-6 is a potent inhibitor of PrP fibril formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the native aggregation assay (NAA).

claim: Syntaxin-6 significantly delayed the lag phase of fibril formation at highly sub-stoichiometric molar ratios.
source: It significantly delayed the lag phase of fibril formation at highly sub-stoichiometric molar ratios.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the aggregation kinetics experiments.

claim: Syntaxin-6 prolonged the presence of neurotoxic PrP species.
source: However, when assessing toxicity of different aggregation time points to primary neurons, syntaxin-6 prolonged the presence of neurotoxic PrP species.
evidence: This claim is supported by toxicity assay data on primary neurons.

claim: In the presence of syntaxin-6, PrP formed less-ordered aggregates containing syntaxin-6 instead of highly ordered fibrils.
source: Electron microscopy and super-resolution fluorescence microscopy revealed that, instead of highly ordered fibrils, in the presence of syntaxin-6 PrP formed less-ordered aggregates containing syntaxin-6.
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy and super-resolution fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: Syntaxin-6 can directly alter the initial phase of PrP self-assembly.
source: These data strongly suggest that the protein can directly alter the initial phase of PrP self-assembly and, uniquely, can act as an 'anti-chaperone', which promotes toxic aggregation intermediates by inhibiting fibril formation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on aggregation kinetics and morphology.

claim: Syntaxin-6 can act as an 'anti-chaperone' which promotes toxic aggregation intermediates by inhibiting fibril formation.
source: These data strongly suggest that the protein can directly alter the initial phase of PrP self-assembly and, uniquely, can act as an 'anti-chaperone', which promotes toxic aggregation intermediates by inhibiting fibril formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing inhibition of fibril formation and prolonged toxicity.

claim: Prion-like mechanisms are believed to drive dozens of human neurodegenerative and systemic diseases.
source: Prion replication and prion-like mechanisms are believed to drive dozens of human neurodegenerative and systemic diseases, as well as scrapie, bovine spongiform encephalopathy, and chronic wasting disease in animals (Prusiner, 1998; Brundin et al., 2010; Frost and Diamond, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Prions are fibrillar assemblies of misfolded cellular prion protein (PrPC) which form highly ordered parallel in register intermolecular β-sheet amyloid structures.
source: Prions are fibrillar assemblies of misfolded cellular prion protein (PrPC), which form highly ordered parallel in register intermolecular β-sheet amyloid structures (prion rods, Manka et al., 2022; Kraus et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Purified prion rods are not directly neurotoxic.
source: While purified prion rods are not directly neurotoxic, prion-associated toxicity can be blocked by anti-PrP antibodies (Benilova et al., 2020; Reilly et al., 2022) suggesting that non-fibrillar PrP assemblies, which form after prion titers plateau (Sandberg et al., 2011; Sandberg et al., 2014; Collinge, 2016), could be the toxic agents, as is the case for other amyloid-forming proteins (Haass and Selkoe, 2007; Corbett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Prion-associated toxicity can be blocked by anti-PrP antibodies.
source: While purified prion rods are not directly neurotoxic, prion-associated toxicity can be blocked by anti-PrP antibodies (Benilova et al., 2020; Reilly et al., 2022) suggesting that non-fibrillar PrP assemblies, which form after prion titers plateau (Sandberg et al., 2011; Sandberg et al., 2014; Collinge, 2016), could be the toxic agents, as is the case for other amyloid-forming proteins (Haass and Selkoe, 2007; Corbett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Non-fibrillar PrP assemblies which form after prion titers plateau could be the toxic agents.
source: While purified prion rods are not directly neurotoxic, prion-associated toxicity can be blocked by anti-PrP antibodies (Benilova et al., 2020; Reilly et al., 2022) suggesting that non-fibrillar PrP assemblies, which form after prion titers plateau (Sandberg et al., 2011; Sandberg et al., 2014; Collinge, 2016), could be the toxic agents, as is the case for other amyloid-forming proteins (Haass and Selkoe, 2007; Corbett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from cited studies and comparison to other amyloid diseases.

claim: Accidental exposure accounts for only a tiny percentage of Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) cases.
source: However, accidental exposure only accounts for a tiny percentage of Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) cases.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological knowledge of CJD.

claim: Mutations in the PRNP gene cause only 10–15% of CJD cases.
source: Similarly, mutations in the PRNP gene, which codes for the prion protein PrP, cause only 10–15% of CJD cases (Mead et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to epidemiological research.

claim: The majority of prion disease cases are sporadic in nature, where PrP is thought to spontaneously misfold.
source: The majority of prion disease cases are sporadic in nature, where PrP is thought to spontaneously misfold.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological knowledge and mechanistic understanding.

claim: A recent genome-wide association study identified two highly significant risk loci for sporadic CJD including one in and near to STX6.
source: A recent genome-wide association study to discover non-PRNP risk factors of sporadic CJD (sCJD) identified two highly significant risk loci including one in and near to STX6 (Jones et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genome-wide association study.

claim: Elevated STX6 mRNA in the caudate and putamen nuclei correlated with CJD risk.
source: Elevated STX6 mRNA in the caudate and putamen nuclei, two regions implicated in CJD pathology (Meissner et al., 2009), correlated with CJD risk.
evidence: This is supported by citation to expression studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 is a 255 amino-acid protein that predominantly localizes to the trans-Golgi network (TGN).
source: STX6 encodes syntaxin-6, an 8-exon, 255 amino-acid protein that predominantly localizes to the trans-Golgi network (TGN), and is mainly involved in recycling of cargo between the TGN and early endosomes (Jung et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to protein characterization studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 is mainly involved in recycling of cargo between the TGN and early endosomes.
source: STX6 encodes syntaxin-6, an 8-exon, 255 amino-acid protein that predominantly localizes to the trans-Golgi network (TGN), and is mainly involved in recycling of cargo between the TGN and early endosomes (Jung et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to functional studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 is thought to form part of the t-SNARE complex involved in the decision of a target membrane to accept the fusion of a vesicle.
source: Syntaxin-6 is thought to form part of the t-SNARE complex involved in the decision of a target membrane to accept the fusion of a vesicle (Wendler and Tooze, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mechanistic studies.

claim: Misfolded prion protein in infected cells localizes at the plasma membrane, the likely site of prion conversion.
source: Misfolded prion protein in infected cells localizes at the plasma membrane, the likely site of prion conversion (Goold et al., 2011), as well as in perinuclear compartments.
evidence: This is supported by citation to cell biology studies.

claim: Early and late endosomes, the endocytic recycling compartment and multivesicular bodies have been implicated as prion replication sites.
source: Early and late endosomes, the endocytic recycling compartment and multivesicular bodies have also been implicated as prion replication sites (Yamasaki et al., 2018; Yim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to cell biology studies.

claim: STX6 is a risk gene for progressive supranuclear palsy.
source: STX6 is also a risk gene for progressive supranuclear palsy (Höglinger et al., 2011), where the protein interacts directly with tau through its transmembrane domain (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to genetic studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 interacts directly with tau through its transmembrane domain.
source: STX6 is also a risk gene for progressive supranuclear palsy (Höglinger et al., 2011), where the protein interacts directly with tau through its transmembrane domain (Lee et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to protein interaction studies.

claim: STX6 has been identified in a proteome-wide association study in Alzheimer's disease.
source: STX6 has been identified in a proteome-wide association study in Alzheimer's disease (Wingo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to proteomics studies.

claim: Downregulation of syntaxin-6 expression in a murine neuroblastoma scrapie cell model (PK1) did not alter PrPC expression and had no obvious effect on PrPC trafficking.
source: Downregulation of syntaxin-6 expression in a murine neuroblastoma scrapie cell model (PK1) did not alter PrPC expression and had no obvious effect on PrPC trafficking (Jones et al., 2020), suggesting that it may directly alter prion replication by a yet undiscovered chaperone-like activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to cell biology experiments.

claim: Syntaxin-6 may directly alter prion replication by a yet undiscovered chaperone-like activity.
source: Downregulation of syntaxin-6 expression in a murine neuroblastoma scrapie cell model (PK1) did not alter PrPC expression and had no obvious effect on PrPC trafficking (Jones et al., 2020), suggesting that it may directly alter prion replication by a yet undiscovered chaperone-like activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the lack of effect on PrPC expression and trafficking.

claim: Chaperones aid and tightly control protein folding and protein homeostasis in the cell.
source: An array of chaperone proteins aid and tightly control protein folding and protein homeostasis in the cell (Hartl, 2011; Balch et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HSP70 inhibits protein misfolding and can delay amyloid formation in vitro and in model organisms.
source: Chaperones, such as the heat shock protein HSP70, inhibit protein misfolding and can delay amyloid formation in vitro (Glover and Lindquist, 1998) and in model organisms (Thackray et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Established fibril formation assays for PrP in vitro require non-physiological conditions such as high temperatures, denaturants, and detergents or low pH.
source: The established fibril formation assays for PrP in vitro require non-physiological conditions, such as high temperatures (Atarashi et al., 2011), denaturants (Legname et al., 2004), and detergents or low pH (Post et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claim: Full-length murine PrPC 23-231 (mPrP23) and human PrPC 23-231 (hPrP23) were expressed recombinantly, purified via Ni-NTA chromatography, and refolded into their native conformation.
source: In order to study PrP fibril formation under near-native conditions in vitro, full-length murine PrPC 23-231 (mPrP23) and human PrPC 23-231 (hPrP23) were expressed recombinantly (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), purified via Ni-NTA chromatography, and refolded into their native conformation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used, with reference to supplementary figures showing the results.

claim: Elevated temperatures accelerated PrP fibril formation.
source: While PrP was slow to form aggregates de novo without the addition of seeds, elevated temperatures accelerated fibril formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) as had been previously observed (Ziaunys et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and citation to previous observations.

claim: Aggregation at 42°C, pH 6.8 yielded highly reproducible conditions for the formation of fibrils.
source: Aggregation at 42°C, pH 6.8 yielded highly reproducible conditions for the formation of fibrils (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C) when agitated by glass or silanized zirconia beads.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Fibrils formed in NAA had diameters of 8–12 nm and morphologies typical of amyloid fibrils.
source: Fibrils had diameters of 8–12 nm and morphologies typical of amyloid fibrils (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in the figures.

claim: Fibrils formed in NAA were resistant to digestion by proteinase K to the same degree as authentic prion rods prepared from RML-infected mice.
source: Fibrils formed in native aggregation assay (NAA) were resistant to digestion by proteinase K to the same degree as authentic prion rods prepared from RML-infected mice, producing a main PK-resistant fragment of ~12 kD (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in the figures.

claim: The addition of preformed fibrillar aggregates as seeds accelerated fibril formation in a concentration-dependent manner by decreasing lag-times.
source: The addition of preformed fibrillar aggregates as seeds accelerated fibril formation in a concentration-dependent manner by decreasing lag-times (t50, Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplements 2D and 3) but had no significant influence on rates of fibril elongation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Lag phases and elongation rates of mPrP23 in vitro were indistinguishable when using synthetic seed formed from recombinant PrPC or using authentic prion rods isolated from mice infected with scrapie strains RML or ME7.
source: Lag phases and elongation rates of mPrP23 in vitro were indistinguishable when using synthetic seed formed from recombinant PrPC or using authentic prion rods, isolated from mice infected with scrapie strains RML or ME7 in (Figure 1—figure supplements 2D, E and 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparative kinetic data shown in the figures.

claim: Fibrils formed from synthetic seeds displayed increased ThT fluorescence when compared to RML and ME7 seeded fibrils, hinting at a difference in fibril structure imprinted by the different seed templates.
source: Interestingly, fibrils formed from synthetic seeds displayed increased ThT fluorescence when compared to RML and ME7 seeded fibrils, hinting at a difference in fibril structure imprinted by the different seed templates (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is an inference based on ThT fluorescence data shown in the figures.

claim: The lag phase of hPrP23 aggregation was largely independent of PrP monomer concentration.
source: The lag phase of hPrP23 aggregation was largely independent of PrP monomer concentration (Figure 1E and F), while elongation rates even showed a slight inverse reaction to monomer concentration (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-dependent kinetic data shown in the figures.

claim: Elongation rates of hPrP23 showed a slight inverse reaction to monomer concentration.
source: The lag phase of hPrP23 aggregation was largely independent of PrP monomer concentration (Figure 1E and F), while elongation rates even showed a slight inverse reaction to monomer concentration (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-dependent kinetic data shown in the figures.

claim: PrP refolding rather than elongation may be rate-limiting under the NAA conditions.
source: Therefore, PrP refolding rather than elongation may be rate-limiting under the assay conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed concentration independence of lag phase and elongation rates.

claim: ThT amplitude at the end of growth was proportional to monomer concentration.
source: ThT amplitude at the end of growth was proportional to monomer concentration (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by concentration-dependent amplitude data shown in the figure.

claim: The lag phase increased and ThT amplitude dropped at monomer concentrations above 16 µM, suggesting the formation of off-pathway PrP aggregates at high monomer concentrations.
source: However, the lag phase increased and ThT amplitude dropped at monomer concentrations above 16 µM, suggesting the formation of off-pathway PrP aggregates at high monomer concentrations, which do not contribute to fibril formation (Powers and Powers, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes at high concentration, supported by citation to similar observations.

claim: Analysis of aggregation kinetics using the Amylofit framework confirmed that the concentration dependence of fibril formation could be described adequately only under the assumption that kinetics were dominated by saturated elongation.
source: Analysis of aggregation kinetics using the Amylofit framework confirmed this interpretation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The concentration dependence of fibril formation could be described adequately only under the assumption that kinetics were dominated by saturated elongation.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic modeling data shown in the figure.

claim: Syntaxin-6 delayed the lag phase of hPrP23 fibril formation even at highly sub-stoichiometric molar ratios of 1:100.
source: To our surprise, syntaxin-6 delayed the lag phase of hPrP23 fibril formation even at highly sub-stoichiometric molar ratios of 1:100 and prevented fibril formation entirely at equimolar ratio (STX6, Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in the figures.

claim: Syntaxin-6 prevented fibril formation entirely at equimolar ratio.
source: To our surprise, syntaxin-6 delayed the lag phase of hPrP23 fibril formation even at highly sub-stoichiometric molar ratios of 1:100 and prevented fibril formation entirely at equimolar ratio (STX6, Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in the figures.

claim: Syntaxin-6 only slightly lowered fibril elongation rates.
source: At the same time, it only slightly lowered fibril elongation rates (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in the figure.

claim: Syntaxin-6 promoted the formation of aggregate clusters rather than distinct amyloid fibrils.
source: Syntaxin-6 promoted the formation of aggregate clusters (Figure 2D and E) rather than distinct amyloid fibrils (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in the figures.

claim: Syntaxin-6 was incorporated into PrP aggregates.
source: Immuno-gold staining revealed that syntaxin-6 was incorporated into these aggregates (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by immuno-gold TEM data shown in the figure.

claim: HSPA1A prevented fibril formation in favor of amorphous PrP aggregates.
source: Similarly, HSPA1A prevented fibril formation in favor of amorphous PrP aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), while hPrP23 formed fibrillar aggregates in the presence of control protein STMN1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: hPrP23 formed fibrillar aggregates in the presence of control protein STMN1.
source: Similarly, HSPA1A prevented fibril formation in favor of amorphous PrP aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), while hPrP23 formed fibrillar aggregates in the presence of control protein STMN1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: Syntaxin-6 delayed but did not prevent the formation of hPrP23 aggregates.
source: However, sedimentation after 0–90 hr incubation revealed that syntaxin-6 delayed but did not prevent the formation of hPrP23 aggregates.
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data.

claim: A substantial fraction of hPrP23 remained soluble when incubated with HSPA1A at a 1:10 molar ratio.
source: In contrast, a substantial fraction of hPrP23 remained soluble when incubated with HSPA1A at a 1:10 molar ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sedimentation assay data shown in the figure.

claim: At sub-stoichiometric ratios, syntaxin-6 delays but does not prevent the formation of seeding competent PrP fibrils.
source: Samples harvested during the lag phase of either reactions were not seeding competent, but both aggregates formed in the presence and absence of syntaxin-6 (1:10) were seeding competent after the formation of ThT-positive aggregates, indicating that, at sub-stoichiometric ratios, syntaxin-6 delays, but does not prevent the formation of seeding competent PrP fibrils.
evidence: This is an inference based on secondary seeding assay data.

claim: The presence of syntaxin-6 lowered the amount of seeding competent aggregates by at least three orders of magnitude.
source: Both in syntaxin-6 and in untreated samples, seeding activity was only found in the total and insoluble fractions. The presence of syntaxin-6 lowered the amount of seeding competent aggregates by at least three orders of magnitude (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C–E and 5).
evidence: This is supported by secondary seeding assay data shown in the figures.

claim: Ionic interactions may mediate the binding of syntaxin-6 to PrP.
source: Syntaxin-6 prolonged the lag phase at low and physiological salt concentrations, but lag phases decreased with increasing NaCl concentration, suggesting that ionic interactions may mediate the binding of syntaxin-6 to PrP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed salt concentration dependence of the effect.

claim: hPrP23 and syntaxin-6 co-aggregated into large aggregate clusters.
source: To visualize the interaction of syntaxin-6 with PrP aggregates and fibrils, we imaged NAA endpoints by dSTORM super-resolution microscopy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) revealing that hPrP23 and syntaxin-6 co-aggregated into large aggregate clusters.
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in the figure.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy indicated a fibrillar substructure of PrP-syntaxin-6 aggregates.
source: Super-resolution microscopy indicated a fibrillar substructure of these aggregates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B) similar to that observed in TEM (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy and TEM data shown in the figures.

claim: Syntaxin-6 preferentially bound to specific 'hotspots' on pre-formed PrP fibrils.
source: When, conversely, syntaxin-6 labeled with AlexaFluor647 was added to pre-formed fibrillar hPrP23 formed under NAA conditions, it preferentially bound to specific 'hotspots' on the PrP fibril (Figure 3A and B, indicated by arrows).
evidence: This is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in the figures.

claim: Interaction sites of syntaxin-6 with PrP fibrils were often located at fibril ends or kinks in the fibril.
source: Interestingly, interaction sites were often located at fibril ends or kinks in the fibril.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy data.

claim: Syntaxin-6 may have a role in fibril breakage or secondary nucleation.
source: Since syntaxin-6 only weakly affected apparent fibril elongation rates in bulk assays, this may suggest a role of syntaxin-6 in fibril breakage or secondary nucleation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the binding pattern and kinetic data.

claim: PrP formed longer, unbranched fibrils with increasing salt concentration.
source: PrP formed longer, unbranched fibrils with increasing salt concentration.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments at different salt concentrations.

claim: Syntaxin-6 induced the formation of aggregate clusters when visualized by TAB imaging when compared with untreated fibrils.
source: As had been seen in TEM, syntaxin-6 induced the formation of aggregate clusters when visualized by TAB imaging (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3) when compared with untreated fibrils, supporting the hypothesis that the protein may alter secondary nucleation/branching of fibrils.
evidence: This is supported by TAB imaging data shown in the figures and supports a hypothesis about mechanism.

claim: Syntaxin-6 and PrP interact via FRET in perinuclear compartments in both non-infected and infected PK1 cells.
source: PixFRET analysis indicated a perinuclear interaction between both proteins, both in non-infected (PK1) and infected (iS7) cells (Figure 4A, wide arrows).
evidence: This is supported by FRET imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: An additional FRET signal on the plasma membrane of infected cells suggests that syntaxin-6 may be recruited into misfolded PrP assemblies.
source: An additional FRET signal on the plasma membrane of infected cells suggests that syntaxin-6 may be recruited into misfolded PrP assemblies (Figure 4A, narrow arrows).
evidence: This is an inference based on FRET imaging data shown in the figure.

claim: Only antibodies directed to the unfolded N-terminal domain of PrP displayed FRET in membrane-associated compartments.
source: This interaction resulted in FRET signals with all three anti-PrP antibodies, whereas only the two antibodies directed to the unfolded N-terminal domain of PrP (5B2 and 6D11) displayed FRET in membrane-associated compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FRET imaging data with different antibodies shown in the figure.

claim: The differential FRET signals may suggest a different binding mode of syntaxin-6 to PrP species in perinuclear versus membrane-associated compartments.
source: This may suggest a different binding mode of syntaxin-6 to PrP species in both compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential FRET signals with different antibodies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 does not directly alter prion replication in vitro under PMCA conditions.
source: Both substrates generated comparable amounts of PK-resistant PrP (Figure 4B), indicating that syntaxin-6 does not directly alter prion replication in vitro under PMCA conditions, which are dominated by fibril fragmentation/elongation.
evidence: This is supported by PMCA data comparing Stx6+/+ and Stx6-/- substrates shown in the figure.

claim: PrP aggregates were highly toxic to primary neurons during lag and early growth phases but neurotoxicity was diminished at the plateau phase of fibril formation.
source: PrP aggregates were highly toxic to primary neurons during lag and early growth phases (20 hr and 40 hr incubation), but neurotoxicity was diminished at the plateau phase of fibril formation, so that endpoint aggregates (90 hr) were no more toxic than PrP monomers or buffer controls (Figure 5A and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by neurotoxicity assay data shown in the figures.

claim: PrP toxicity preceded the formation of seeding-competent assemblies, supporting the hypothesis that the toxic PrP species is a pre-fibrillar assembly.
source: Notably, PrP toxicity preceded the formation of seeding-competent assemblies (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), supporting the hypothesis that the toxic PrP species is a pre-fibrillar assembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal relationship between toxicity and seeding competence.

claim: PrP aggregated in the presence of syntaxin-6 retained its neurotoxicity significantly longer than PrP incubated in the absence of syntaxin-6.
source: In contrast, PrP aggregated in the presence of syntaxin-6 (1:0.1 molar ratio) retained its neurotoxicity significantly longer than PrP incubated in the absence of syntaxin-6 (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by neurotoxicity assay data shown in the figures.

claim: PrP was significantly more toxic in the presence of syntaxin-6 at later time points when PrP would form fibrils in the absence of syntaxin-6.
source: While PrP species formed early in the lag phase of aggregation at 20 hr were neurotoxic both in the presence and absence of syntaxin-6 when compared to t = 0 hr, PrP was significantly more toxic in the presence of syntaxin-6 at later time points when PrP would form fibrils in the absence of syntaxin-6 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by neurotoxicity assay data shown in the figures.

claim: In delaying or preventing PrP fibril formation, syntaxin-6 prolonged the presence of toxic aggregation intermediates and exacerbated neurotoxicity.
source: Thus, in delaying or preventing PrP fibril formation, syntaxin-6 prolonged the presence of toxic aggregation intermediates and exacerbated neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined kinetic and toxicity data.

claim: Full-length PrP formed fibrils with morphology and β-sheet secondary structure characteristic of amyloid under NAA conditions.
source: Full-length PrP formed fibrils with morphology and β-sheet secondary structure characteristic of amyloid under conditions of the NAA (Willbold et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by structural characterization data and citation.

claim: Fibril formation in NAA displayed sigmoid aggregation kinetics typical of a nucleated polymerization mechanism.
source: Fibril formation could be tracked by binding of the amyloidophilic dye ThT and displayed sigmoid aggregation kinetics typical of a nucleated polymerization mechanism (Cohen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data and citation to established mechanisms.

claim: The limiting dilution for seeding in NAA was ~10–10 (w/w), which corresponds to approximately 2000 PrP molecules per well or 5 prion rods of a typical length of 200 nm.
source: The limiting dilution for seeding was ~10–10 (w/w), which corresponds to approximately 2000 PrP molecules per well or 5 prion rods of a typical length of 200 nm (Terry et al., 2016), similar to other seeding assays (Stöhr et al., 2008; Atarashi et al., 2007; Du et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by seeding dilution data and citations to similar assays.

claim: In NAA, monomer refolding was rate-limiting for fibril elongation.
source: In NAA, both lag phase t50 and elongation rate constant k displayed little dependence on monomer concentration, which suggests that monomer refolding was rate-limiting for fibril elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed concentration independence.

claim: Elongation saturates at high monomer concentration as conformational change of PrP becomes rate-limiting.
source: While in general aggregation kinetics scale with monomer concentration, elongation saturates at high monomer concentration as conformational change of PrP becomes rate-limiting (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008; Honda and Kuwata, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: High salt concentration shields charges, which promotes hydrophobic interactions and lowers the critical concentration of nucleated polymerization, often leading to the formation of amyloid fibril clusters.
source: High salt concentration shields charges, which promotes hydrophobic interactions and lowers the critical concentration of nucleated polymerization, often leading to the formation of amyloid fibril clusters (Klement et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The effect of syntaxin-6 on PrP aggregation was similar to that of HSP70.
source: On the face, its effect was similar to that of the heat shock protein family A (HSP70) member 1A (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which would suggest a role of syntaxin-6 as a potent aggregation inhibitor with chaperone-like activity.
evidence: This is a comparison based on experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: HSP70 has been described as a 'holdase' which inhibits amyloid formation of various proteins at sub-stoichiometric concentrations even in the absence of ATP by binding to early-stage aggregation intermediates.
source: HSP70 has been described as a 'holdase', which inhibits amyloid formation of various proteins at sub-stoichiometric concentrations even in the absence of ATP by binding to early-stage aggregation intermediates (Evans et al., 2006; Wacker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression or exogenous addition of HSP70 rescued cytotoxicity in cell cultures and model organisms.
source: Overexpression or exogenous addition of HSP70 rescued cytotoxicity in cell cultures and model organisms (Rosas et al., 2016; Bongiovanni et al., 2018; Fernandez-Funez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Sequestering aggregation intermediates into inert off-pathway aggregates can be a powerful strategy against amyloid toxicity.
source: Sequestering aggregation intermediates into inert off-pathway aggregates can be a powerful strategy against amyloid toxicity (Bieschke et al., 2010; Ehrnhoefer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Natural and chemical chaperones can detoxify aggregation intermediates by promoting fibril formation and stabilizing mature amyloid fibrils.
source: Conversely, natural and chemical chaperones can detoxify aggregation intermediates by promoting fibril formation and stabilizing mature amyloid fibrils (Cohen et al., 2006; Bieschke et al., 2012; Lam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Brain homogenates from scrapie-infected mice have a specific toxic component which can be blocked by the addition of anti-PrP antibody.
source: Brain homogenates from scrapie-infected mice have a specific toxic component, which can be blocked by the addition of anti-PrP antibody (Benilova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental studies.

claim: Highly purified infectious prion rods were shown not to be directly neurotoxic.
source: However, highly purified infectious prion rods were shown not to be directly neurotoxic (Benilova et al., 2020), suggesting that toxicity may be caused by non-prion assemblies, which accumulate after the infectious titer has peaked and which, unlike prions, are sensitive to sarkosyl (Reilly et al., 2022; Sandberg et al., 2011; Sandberg et al., 2014) or by transient aggregation intermediates, whose formation may be catalyzed by prions or other fibrillar PrP assemblies (Collinge and Clarke, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The chaperone Brichos breaks generation of toxic Aβ oligomers which are formed through surface-catalyzed secondary nucleation.
source: The chaperone Brichos breaks generation of toxic Aβ oligomers, which are formed through surface-catalyzed secondary nucleation (Cohen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mechanistic studies.

claim: PrP itself binds to and inhibits the elongation of Aβ amyloid fibrils.
source: PrP itself binds to and inhibits the elongation of Aβ amyloid fibrils (Amin and Harris, 2021; Bove-Fenderson et al., 2017) oligomers and nanotubes.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The presence of PrP during Aβ aggregation led to the formation of larger numbers of shorter fibrils and increased Aβ neurotoxicity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The presence of PrP during aggregation led to the formation of larger numbers of shorter fibrils and increased Aβ neurotoxicity in a dose-dependent manner (Amin and Harris, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to experimental studies.

claim: PrP may exacerbate neurotoxicity in a mechanism similar to syntaxin-6.
source: This suggests that PrP not only acts as a receptor for toxic amyloid oligomers (Freir et al., 2011; Nicoll et al., 2013), but may exacerbate neurotoxicity in a mechanism similar to syntaxin-6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of effects and citations to receptor studies.

claim: Previous studies found only weak binding of syntaxin-6 to monomeric PrPC.
source: Notably, syntaxin-6, when added to preformed fibrils, preferentially bound to fibril ends and other hotspots (Figure 3). Previous studies found only weak binding of syntaxin-6 to monomeric PrPC (Jones et al., 2020), which, together with the inhibition at sub-stoichiometric concentrations, strongly suggests an interaction with early aggregation intermediates and with fibrillary assemblies, possibly promoting secondary nucleation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to binding studies.

claim: The weak binding to monomeric PrPC and inhibition at sub-stoichiometric concentrations strongly suggests syntaxin-6 interacts with early aggregation intermediates and with fibrillary assemblies, possibly promoting secondary nucleation.
source: Previous studies found only weak binding of syntaxin-6 to monomeric PrPC (Jones et al., 2020), which, together with the inhibition at sub-stoichiometric concentrations, strongly suggests an interaction with early aggregation intermediates and with fibrillary assemblies, possibly promoting secondary nucleation.
evidence: This is an inference based on binding data and kinetic observations.

claim: Deletion of syntaxin-6 only modestly delayed the incubation period in RML prion infected mice.
source: While variants at the STX6 locus are known risk factors for sCJD (Jones et al., 2020), its deletion only modestly delayed the incubation period in RML prion infected mice, an observation that is open to different interpretations (Hill, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to in vivo studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 may confer risk of disease by either facilitating the initial generation of prions in sporadic disease or exacerbating prion-associated toxicity.
source: Rather than directly altering prion replication kinetics, the protein may confer risk of disease by either facilitating the initial generation of prions in sporadic disease or exacerbating prion-associated toxicity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: The finding that syntaxin-6 exacerbated toxicity argues against the hypothesis that syntaxin-6 binding to mature PrP fibrils induces fibril breakage.
source: This finding argues against the hypothesis that syntaxin-6 binding to mature PrP fibrils induces fibril breakage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PMCA results.

claim: An increase in fibrils branching/secondary nucleation as observed in the presence of syntaxin-6 would have little effect on replication kinetics dominated by fragmentation/elongation.
source: Correspondingly, an increase in fibrils branching/secondary nucleation as observed in the presence of syntaxin-6 (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 3) would have little effect on replication kinetics dominated by fragmentation/elongation.
evidence: This is an inference based on mechanistic understanding and microscopy observations.

claim: PrPC is present mainly in the TGN and on the outer plasma membrane.
source: PrPC is present mainly in the TGN and on the outer plasma membrane, while mature PrPC is tethered to the membrane by a C-terminal glycophosphadityl-inositol anchor.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPC localization.

claim: At the plasma membrane, PrPC is incorporated into lipid rafts and caveolae.
source: At the plasma membrane, PrPC is incorporated into lipid rafts and caveolae, which are membrane microdomains enriched in cholesterol and sphingolipids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PrPC membrane localization.

claim: PrPC has been detected in multi-vesicular bodies and, to a small degree, in the cytosol.
source: However, it has also been detected in multi-vesicular bodies and, to a small degree, in the cytosol (Grassmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to cell biology studies.

claim: Both lipid rafts and the endocytic pathway are implicated as sites of prion replication.
source: Both lipid rafts and the endocytic pathway are implicated as sites of prion replication (Grassmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mechanistic studies.

claim: Syntaxin-6 has a role in caveolin membrane recycling.
source: Interestingly, syntaxin-6 has role in caveolin membrane recycling (Choudhury et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to functional studies.

claim: Both PrP and syntaxin-6 contain a trans-membrane domain and PrP can populate transmembrane forms in neurons.
source: Both PrP and syntaxin-6 contain a trans-membrane domain and PrP can populate transmembrane forms in neurons (Hegde et al., 1998; Stewart and Harris, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: PrP and prions bound to the membrane bilayer could interact with the transmembrane domain of syntaxin-6, similar to the tau protein.
source: It is therefore plausible that, similar to the tau protein, PrP and prions bound to the membrane bilayer could interact with the transmembrane domain of syntaxin-6.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural considerations and analogy to tau.

claim: Amyloid assemblies can disrupt membrane integrity through mechanical rupture, pore formation, or altering membrane curvature.
source: Amyloid assemblies can disrupt membrane integrity through mechanical rupture, pore formation, or altering membrane curvature (Shi et al., 2015; Lashuel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Disruption of membranes on the cell surface and in vesicles of the endocytic pathway is a central step in the internalization of misfolded polypeptides such as Aβ.
source: Disruption of membranes on the cell surface and in vesicles of the endocytic pathway is a central step in the internalization of other misfolded polypeptides, such as Aβ (Jin et al., 2016; Friedrich et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mechanistic studies.

claim: Membrane disruption has been hypothesized to be necessary for cellular prion propagation.
source: Similarly, it has been hypothesized to be necessary for cellular prion propagation (Yim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: FRET imaging suggests a direct contact between PrP and syntaxin-6 in a membrane-associated compartment in prion-infected cells.
source: FRET imaging suggests a direct contact between PrP and syntaxin-6 in a membrane-associated compartment in prion-infected cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), supporting this hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by FRET imaging data shown in the figures.

claim: Genetic variants in or near to STX6 that enhance brain expression of the protein might modify the risk of CJD by direct interaction with PrP and changing aggregation pathways.
source: Genetic variants in or near to STX6 that enhance brain expression of the protein might therefore modify the risk of CJD by direct interaction with PrP and changing aggregation pathways, including the possibility of favoring more toxic aggregation intermediates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the combined genetic and experimental findings.
